sub: Covers basics, scope and hoisting, closures, `this`, prototypes, async JS (callbacks, promises, async/await, event loop), ES6+ features, DOM and the output-based questions interviewers love.

q.q: What is JavaScript and where does it run?
a: JavaScript is a high-level, single-threaded, dynamically typed programming language. It was made for web pages, so it runs in every browser, but with **Node.js** it also runs on servers.
It is used to make pages interactive, build backends, mobile apps (React Native) and even desktop apps (Electron).

q.q: What are the data types in JavaScript?
a: There are 8 types. Seven are **primitive**: `string`, `number`, `bigint`, `boolean`, `undefined`, `null`, `symbol`. The eighth is **object** (arrays, functions, dates are all objects).
Primitives are copied by value; objects are copied by reference.

q.q: What is the difference between `var`, `let` and `const`?
a: `var` is function-scoped, can be re-declared, and is hoisted with value `undefined`.
`let` is block-scoped (inside `{ }`), cannot be re-declared in the same scope, and is in the "temporal dead zone" until its line runs.
`const` is like `let` but cannot be re-assigned. The object it points to can still change.
Say "I use const by default, let when the value changes, and avoid var."

q.q: What is the difference between `==` and `===`?
a: `==` compares after converting types (loose equality). `===` compares value AND type with no conversion (strict equality).

5 == "5"    // true
5 === "5"   // false
null == undefined   // true
null === undefined  // false

q.q: What is the difference between `null` and `undefined`?
a: `undefined` means a variable was declared but no value was given. `null` is a value you set on purpose to say "empty".
`typeof undefined` is "undefined" but `typeof null` is "object" (an old bug in JS).

q.q: What is `NaN`? How do you check for it?
a: `NaN` means "Not a Number", the result of a bad math operation like `"abc" * 2`. Strangely, `NaN === NaN` is false, so use `Number.isNaN(x)` to check.

q.q: What is type coercion?
a: Coercion is JavaScript automatically converting one type into another.
`+` with a string joins text; other math operators convert to numbers.

q.q: What are truthy and falsy values?
a: Falsy values become `false` in an if-condition. There are only a few: `false`, `0`, `-0`, `0n`, `""`, `null`, `undefined`, `NaN`. Everything else is truthy, including `"0"`, `[]` and `{}`.

q.q: What is the difference between primitive and reference types?
a: Primitives (number, string...) are stored directly and copied by value. Objects and arrays are stored as a reference (address), so copying the variable copies the address, and both variables point to the same object.

let a = [1]; let b = a; b.push(2);
console.log(a); // [1, 2]

q.q: What is hoisting?
a: Hoisting means declarations are moved to the top of their scope before code runs.
`let`/`const` are hoisted but not initialised (accessing them early gives a ReferenceError).
Function declarations are fully hoisted, so you can call them before you write them.

q.q: What is the Temporal Dead Zone (TDZ)?
a: The TDZ is the time between entering a scope and the line where a `let` or `const` variable is declared. Using the variable inside this zone throws a ReferenceError.

q.q: What is scope? What are its types?
a: Scope decides where a variable can be accessed.
**Function scope**: available only inside that function.
JavaScript uses **lexical scope**, which means inner functions can use variables of outer functions based on where the code is written.

q.q: What is a closure? Give an example.
a: A closure is when an inner function remembers the variables of its outer function, even after the outer function has finished running.
Uses: data privacy, counters, memoization, and event handlers.
This is the #1 JS question in fresher interviews. Be ready to write this counter example.

q.q: What is the output of this loop and why?
a: It prints `3 3 3`. `var` is function-scoped, so all three callbacks share the same `i`, which is 3 when they finally run. Changing `var` to `let` prints `0 1 2`, because `let` creates a new `i` for each loop iteration.

q.q: What is an IIFE?
a: An Immediately Invoked Function Expression is a function that runs as soon as it is defined. It was used to create a private scope before `let` existed.

q.q: What is the scope chain?
a: When JS looks for a variable, it first checks the current scope, then the outer scope, and so on up to the global scope. This lookup path is called the scope chain. If it is not found anywhere, you get a ReferenceError.

q.q: What is the difference between a normal function and an arrow function?
a: Arrow functions have no own `this`; they take `this` from the surrounding code.
They cannot be used as constructors with `new`.
They have shorter syntax: `const add = (a, b) => a + b;`

q.q: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression?
a: A declaration (`function f() {}`) is hoisted fully. An expression (`const f = function () {}`) is not usable before its line, because only the variable is hoisted.

q.q: What are first-class functions?
a: In JavaScript, functions are treated like any other value. You can store them in variables, pass them as arguments, and return them from other functions.

q.q: What is a higher-order function?
a: A function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function. `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `setTimeout` and `addEventListener` are all higher-order functions.

q.q: What is a callback function?
a: A callback is a function passed into another function to be called later, often when some task finishes.
Too many nested callbacks lead to "callback hell", which promises solve.

q.q: What is currying?
a: Currying converts a function with many arguments into a chain of functions taking one argument each.

const add = a => b => c => a + b + c;
add(1)(2)(3); // 6

q.q: What are default parameters and rest parameters?
a: Default parameters give a value if none is passed: `function hi(name = "Guest") {}`.
Rest parameters collect remaining arguments into an array: `function sum(...nums) { return nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0); }`

q.q: What is the difference between the spread and rest operator?
a: Both use `...`. **Spread** expands an array or object into individual items (`[...arr, 4]`, `{...obj}`). **Rest** collects many items into one array (in function parameters or destructuring).

q.q: What are pure functions?
a: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and does not change anything outside itself (no side effects). Pure functions are easy to test and are central to React and Redux.

q.q: What is `this` in JavaScript?
a: `this` refers to the object that is calling the function. Its value depends on how the function is called:
In a normal function call (non-strict mode), it is the global object; in strict mode it is `undefined`.
In an arrow function, it is taken from the outer scope.
With `new`, it is the newly created object.

q.q: What is the difference between `call`, `apply` and `bind`?
a: All three set the value of `this`.
`call(thisArg, a, b)` calls the function immediately with arguments one by one.
`apply(thisArg, [a, b])` calls immediately with arguments as an array.
`bind(thisArg)` returns a new function with `this` fixed, to be called later.

q.q: What is prototypal inheritance?
a: Every JS object has a hidden link to another object called its **prototype**. If a property is not found on the object, JS looks at its prototype, then the prototype's prototype, and so on (the prototype chain). This is how objects inherit methods, e.g. every array gets `push` from `Array.prototype`.

q.q: What are classes in JavaScript?
a: Classes (ES6) are a cleaner syntax over prototypes.

q.q: What is the difference between shallow copy and deep copy?
a: A shallow copy copies only the top level; nested objects are still shared. A deep copy copies everything.

q.q: What is destructuring?
a: A short way to pull values out of arrays or objects into variables.

const { name, age } = user;
const [first, second] = [10, 20];

q.q: What is the difference between `Object.freeze` and `Object.seal`?
a: `freeze` makes an object fully read-only: no add, delete or change. `seal` stops adding or deleting properties but still allows changing existing ones. Both are shallow.

q.q: What is optional chaining and nullish coalescing?
a: Optional chaining `?.` stops and returns `undefined` if something is null/undefined, instead of crashing: `user?.address?.city`.
Nullish coalescing `??` gives a default only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`: `count ?? 0`. Unlike `||`, it keeps `0` and `""`.

q.q: What is the difference between `map`, `filter` and `reduce`?
a: `map` transforms every item and returns a new array of the same length.
`filter` keeps only items that pass a condition.
`reduce` combines all items into one value (sum, object, etc.).

const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
nums.map(n => n * 2);              // [2,4,6,8]
nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);     // [2,4]
nums.reduce((sum, n) => sum + n, 0); // 10

q.q: What is the difference between `forEach` and `map`?
a: `forEach` just runs a function on each item and returns `undefined`. `map` returns a new array. Use `map` when you need the result.

q.q: What is the difference between `slice` and `splice`?
a: `slice(start, end)` returns a copy of part of the array and does not change the original. `splice(start, count, ...items)` changes the original array by removing or adding items.

q.q: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
a: A `Set` only stores unique values, and spread turns it back into an array.

q.q: How do you reverse a string in JavaScript?
a: Split into characters, reverse the array, then join back.

q.q: What is the difference between `for...in` and `for...of`?
a: `for...in` loops over the **keys** (property names) of an object. `for...of` loops over the **values** of an iterable like an array, string, Map or Set.

q.q: What are Map and Set?
a: `Map` stores key-value pairs where keys can be any type and order is kept. `Set` stores unique values. Both have `.size`, `.has()`, `.delete()` and are faster than objects for frequent add/remove.

q.q: What is the event loop?
a: JavaScript is single-threaded, so it runs one thing at a time on the **call stack**. Slow tasks like timers and network calls are handed to the browser/Node APIs. When they finish, their callbacks go into a queue. The **event loop** keeps checking: if the call stack is empty, it moves the next callback from the queue to the stack.
There are two queues: the **microtask queue** (promises) runs first, then the **macrotask queue** (setTimeout, setInterval, I/O).

q.q: What is the output of this code?
a: Output: `A D C B`. Synchronous code runs first (A, D). Then microtasks (promise: C). Then macrotasks (setTimeout: B), even with 0 ms delay.

q.q: What is a Promise?
a: A Promise is an object that represents a value that will be available in the future. It has three states: **pending**, **fulfilled** (resolved) and **rejected**.

q.q: What is async/await?
a: `async`/`await` is a cleaner way to write promise code so it looks synchronous. An `async` function always returns a promise. `await` pauses the function until the promise settles.

q.q: What is callback hell and how do you avoid it?
a: Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks that are hard to read and debug (the "pyramid of doom"). Avoid it with promises, async/await, and by splitting code into small named functions.

q.q: What is the difference between `Promise.all`, `Promise.allSettled`, `Promise.race` and `Promise.any`?
a: `all`: waits for all; fails fast if any one rejects.
`allSettled`: waits for all and gives every result, success or failure.
`race`: settles with the first promise that settles (success or failure).
`any`: resolves with the first success; rejects only if all fail.

q.q: What is the difference between `setTimeout` and `setInterval`?
a: `setTimeout` runs a function once after a delay. `setInterval` runs it again and again at a fixed interval until you call `clearInterval`.

q.q: How does `fetch` work?
a: `fetch(url)` makes an HTTP request and returns a promise of a Response. You then call `res.json()` (also a promise) to read the body. Note: `fetch` does not reject on 404 or 500; check `res.ok`.

q.q: What is the DOM?
a: The Document Object Model is a tree of objects that the browser creates from your HTML. JavaScript uses it to read and change the page, e.g. `document.getElementById("title").textContent = "Hi"`.

q.q: What is event bubbling and event capturing?
a: When you click an element, the event travels in two phases. **Capturing** goes from the top (window) down to the target. **Bubbling** goes from the target back up to the top. By default, listeners run in the bubbling phase. `event.stopPropagation()` stops it.

q.q: What is event delegation?
a: Instead of adding a listener to every child, you add one listener to the parent and check `event.target`. It works because of bubbling. It saves memory and works for elements added later.

q.q: What is the difference between `localStorage`, `sessionStorage` and cookies?
a: `sessionStorage`: same size, cleared when the tab closes.
Cookies: about 4 KB, sent to the server with every request, can have an expiry, used for sessions/auth.

q.q: What is debouncing and throttling?
a: Both limit how often a function runs.
**Debounce**: run only after the user stops doing something for X ms (search box).
**Throttle**: run at most once every X ms (scroll, resize).

q.q: What is the difference between `e.preventDefault()` and `e.stopPropagation()`?
a: `preventDefault` stops the browser's default action (like a form submitting or a link opening). `stopPropagation` stops the event from bubbling up to parent elements.

q.q: What are the main ES6 features?
a: `let`/`const`, arrow functions, template literals, destructuring, default/rest/spread, classes, modules (`import`/`export`), promises, `Map`/`Set`, and `for...of`.

q.q: What are template literals?
a: Strings written with backticks that allow variables and multi-line text: `` `Hello ${name}` ``.

q.q: What is the difference between CommonJS and ES Modules?
a: CommonJS uses `require()` and `module.exports` and loads synchronously (old Node style). ES Modules use `import`/`export`, are the standard in browsers, and are loaded statically, which allows tree-shaking.

q.q: What is strict mode?
a: Adding `"use strict"` makes JS catch common mistakes, like using undeclared variables or duplicate parameter names. ES modules and classes are strict by default.

q.q: What is memoization?
a: Memoization caches the result of a function call so the same input does not need to be computed again. It is built using a closure and an object/Map as the cache.

q.q: How is JavaScript different from Java?
a: They are unrelated languages. JS is dynamically typed, interpreted/JIT-compiled, and prototype-based. Java is statically typed, compiled to bytecode, and class-based. The name was a marketing decision.

q.q: What is HTML?
a: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the standard language used to create the structure of web pages. It uses tags to tell the browser what each piece of content is: a heading, a paragraph, an image, a link and so on. HTML gives structure, CSS gives style, and JavaScript gives behaviour.

q.q: What is the basic structure of an HTML document?
a: Hello
`<head>` holds information about the page (title, meta, CSS links). `<body>` holds what users see.

q.q: What is `<!DOCTYPE html>`?
a: It tells the browser that the page uses HTML5, so the browser renders it in "standards mode". Without it, the browser may switch to "quirks mode" and display things inconsistently. It is not an HTML tag, it is an instruction.

q.q: What are attributes?
a: Attributes give extra information about an element and are written inside the opening tag as name="value". Examples: `href` in ``, `src` and `alt` in ``, `id`, `class`, `type`.

q.q: What is the difference between `id` and `class`?
a: An `id` must be unique on a page and identifies one element (`#header` in CSS). A `class` can be used on many elements to group them for styling (`.card` in CSS). One element can have many classes but only one id.

q.q: What are the heading tags?
a: `<h1>` to `<h6>`. `<h1>` is the most important (usually one per page, the main title) and `<h6>` the least. Search engines and screen readers use headings to understand the page outline, so do not skip levels just for size.

a:
Block elements start on a new line and take the full width available (`

q.q: What is the difference between `<div>` and `<span>`?
a: Both are generic containers with no meaning. `<div>` is block-level and used to group sections. `<span>` is inline and used to style a small part of text.

q.q: What is semantic HTML? Why is it important?
a: Semantic tags describe the meaning of their content, not just how it looks. Examples: `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, `<section>`, `<article>`, `<aside>`, `<footer>`, `<figure>`.
Benefits: better SEO (search engines understand the page), better accessibility (screen readers can navigate), and cleaner, easier-to-read code.

q.q: What is the difference between `<section>` and `<article>`?
a: `<article>` is self-contained content that makes sense on its own, like a blog post or a product card. `<section>` groups related content under a theme, usually with a heading, like a "Features" section of a page.

q.q: What is the difference between `<b>` and `<strong>`, `<i>` and `<em>`?
a: `<b>` and `<i>` only change looks (bold, italic). `<strong>` means "important" and `<em>` means "emphasis"; screen readers may stress them. Prefer `<strong>` and `<em>` for meaning.

q.q: What is the use of `<main>`?
a: `<main>` wraps the main unique content of the page, excluding the header, nav and footer. There should be only one visible `<main>` per page. It helps screen-reader users jump straight to the content.

q.q: How do you create a link that opens in a new tab?
a: `target="_blank"` opens a new tab; `rel="noopener noreferrer"` is a security best practice so the new page cannot control your page.

q.q: What are the types of lists in HTML?
How do you create a table?
a: `<tr>` = row, `<th>` = header cell, `<td>` = data cell. `colspan` and `rowspan` merge cells.

q.q: Why is the `alt` attribute important on images?
a: `alt` gives a text description of the image. It is read by screen readers, shown if the image fails to load, and used by search engines. Decorative images should have `alt=""`.

q.q: How do you add audio and video in HTML5?
a: `controls` shows play/pause buttons. You can add `autoplay`, `muted`, `loop` and multiple `<source>` tags for different formats.

q.q: What is an `<iframe>`?
a: An iframe embeds another web page inside your page, like a YouTube video or a Google Map. It should be used carefully, since loading other sites can affect security and speed.

q.q: What is the difference between `` and ``?
a: `` shows a single image. `` lets you give multiple `` options so the browser picks the best one by screen size or format (like WebP), with `` as a fallback.

q.q: What is `srcset`?
a: `srcset` lets you list several versions of an image at different sizes. The browser picks the right one for the screen, so mobile users download smaller files.

q.q: How do you create a form in HTML?
a:
<form action="/signup" method="POST">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input type="email" id="email" name="email" required>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
`action` is where data is sent, `method` is GET or POST, and `name` is the key the server receives.

q.q: What is the difference between GET and POST in forms?
a: GET sends data in the URL (visible, limited length, can be bookmarked; good for search). POST sends data in the request body (not shown in URL, no size limit; used for login, signup, uploads).

q.q: What are some HTML5 input types?
a: `email`, `password`, `number`, `tel`, `url`, `date`, `time`, `color`, `range`, `file`, `checkbox`, `radio`, `search`. They give built-in validation and the right mobile keyboard.

q.q: What are form validation attributes?
a: `required`, `minlength`, `maxlength`, `min`, `max`, `pattern` (regex) and `type="email"`. The browser checks these before submitting. Always validate again on the server, since users can bypass browser checks.

q.q: Why use the `<label>` tag?
a: A label describes an input. Linking it with `for="id"` lets users click the label to focus the input, and screen readers announce it. It improves accessibility and usability.

q.q: What is the difference between `readonly` and `disabled`?
a: `readonly` inputs cannot be edited but are still submitted with the form and can be focused. `disabled` inputs cannot be edited, cannot be focused and are NOT submitted.

q.q: What is the difference between radio buttons and checkboxes?
a: Radio buttons (same `name`) allow only one choice from a group. Checkboxes allow selecting zero, one or many options.

q.q: What are `<select>`, `<textarea>` and `<datalist>`?
a: `<select>` makes a dropdown with `<option>`s. `<textarea>` is a multi-line text box. `<datalist>` gives suggestions for an `<input>` while still allowing free typing.

q.q: What are meta tags?
a: Meta tags in `<head>` give information about the page to browsers and search engines. Common ones:
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`: makes the page responsive on mobile.
`<meta name="description" content="...">`: summary shown in search results.

q.q: What is the viewport meta tag and why is it needed?
a: Without it, mobile browsers show the page as a zoomed-out desktop page. `width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0` tells the browser to use the device's real width, which is required for responsive design.

q.q: How does HTML help with SEO?
a: Use a clear `<title>` and meta description, one `<h1>`, proper heading order, semantic tags, `alt` text on images, meaningful link text, and fast-loading pages. Open Graph meta tags control how links look when shared on social media.

q.q: What is the difference between `async` and `defer` on script tags?
a: Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing.
`async` runs the script as soon as it downloads, in any order. Good for independent scripts like analytics.
`defer` runs scripts after HTML parsing is complete, in order. Good for your main app scripts.
A normal `<script>` blocks parsing while it downloads and runs, which is why scripts were often placed at the end of `<body>`.

q.q: Where should you put `<link>` (CSS) and `<script>` tags?
a: CSS `<link>` goes in the `<head>` so the page renders styled from the start. Scripts go at the end of `<body>` or in the `<head>` with `defer`.

q.q: What are the new features in HTML5?
a: Semantic tags, `<audio>` and `<video>`, `<canvas>` and SVG support, new input types and validation, `localStorage`/`sessionStorage`, Geolocation API, drag and drop, Web Workers, and `data-*` attributes.

q.q: What are `data-*` attributes?
a: Custom attributes to store extra data on an element, which JS can read through `dataset`.

q.q: What is the difference between `<canvas>` and `<svg>`?
a: `<canvas>` draws pixels using JavaScript, so it is fast for games and many moving objects, but the drawing is not a set of elements. SVG is vector, made of DOM elements, scales without blurring, and is good for icons, logos and charts.

q.q: What is Web Storage?
a: `localStorage` and `sessionStorage` let you store key-value strings in the browser. `localStorage.setItem("theme", "dark")`, `localStorage.getItem("theme")`. localStorage stays after closing; sessionStorage clears when the tab closes.

q.q: What are Web Workers?
a: Web Workers run JavaScript in a background thread so heavy work does not freeze the page. They cannot access the DOM directly and talk to the main page using messages.

q.q: What is the Geolocation API?
a: `navigator.geolocation.getCurrentPosition(success, error)` gets the user's location after they give permission. It only works on secure (HTTPS) pages.

q.q: What is web accessibility (a11y)?
a: Making websites usable by everyone, including people with disabilities. Key practices: semantic HTML, `alt` text, labels for inputs, keyboard navigation, enough colour contrast, and ARIA attributes when needed.

q.q: What are ARIA attributes?
a: ARIA (Accessible Rich Internet Applications) attributes add extra meaning for screen readers, like `aria-label`, `aria-hidden`, `aria-expanded` and `role="button"`. Rule: use native HTML elements first and ARIA only when HTML cannot do it.

q.q: What is `tabindex`?
a: `tabindex` controls keyboard focus order. `tabindex="0"` makes an element focusable in normal order, `tabindex="-1"` makes it focusable only by JS, and positive values should be avoided.

q.q: What happens when you type a URL in the browser and press Enter?
a: 1. The browser finds the IP address of the domain using DNS.
2. It opens a TCP connection (and a TLS handshake for HTTPS).
4. The server sends back the HTML.
5. The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, calculates layout, and paints pixels on the screen. Scripts and images are loaded along the way.
This is asked in almost every web interview. Mention DNS, TCP, HTTP, and DOM + CSSOM → render.

q.q: What is the critical rendering path?
a: The steps the browser takes to show a page: HTML → DOM, CSS → CSSOM, DOM + CSSOM → render tree, layout (positions and sizes), and paint. Making CSS small and deferring scripts makes this path faster.

q.q: What is the difference between HTML and XHTML?
a: XHTML is a stricter, XML-based version of HTML: all tags must be closed, lowercase, and properly nested. HTML5 is more forgiving and is what everyone uses today.

q.q: What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?
a: HTML5 is the latest version. It added semantic tags, native audio/video, canvas, new form inputs, local storage and many JS APIs, and it uses the simple `<!DOCTYPE html>`.

q.q: What are HTML entities?
a: Special codes to display reserved characters: `<` for <, `>` for >, `&` for &, ` ` for a non-breaking space, `©` for ©.

q.q: What is the difference between `<link>` and `<a>`?
a: `<link>` lives in `<head>` and connects a resource like a stylesheet or favicon; users do not click it. `<a>` is a clickable hyperlink in the page body.

q.q: What is CSS and what are the ways to add it?
a: CSS (Cascading Style Sheets) controls how HTML looks: colours, layout, fonts and spacing. Three ways:

**Inline**: `

**External**: a separate `.css` file linked with `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` (best practice).

q.q: What does "cascading" mean in CSS?
a: When more than one rule applies to the same element, CSS decides which one wins based on importance (`!important`), specificity, and source order (later rules win if all else is equal). This flow of rules is the cascade.

Example: `#nav .link` beats `.nav .link`. `!important` overrides all of these, but avoid it.

q.q: What are the types of selectors?
a: Descendant `div p`, child `div > p`, adjacent sibling `h1 + p`, general sibling `h1 ~ p`

q.q: What is the difference between pseudo-classes and pseudo-elements?
a: A pseudo-class selects an element in a special **state**: `:hover`, `:focus`, `:first-child`, `:nth-child(odd)`. A pseudo-element styles a **part** of an element or adds content: `::before`, `::after`, `::first-letter`, `::placeholder`. Pseudo-elements use double colons.

q.q: What is inheritance in CSS?
a: Some properties pass from a parent to its children automatically, like `color`, `font-family` and `line-height`. Others, like `margin`, `padding`, `border` and `width`, are not inherited. You can force it with `inherit`.

q.q: Explain the CSS box model.
a: Every element is a rectangular box made of four layers from inside to outside:
**Margin**: space outside the border, separating it from other elements.
Draw the four boxes on paper if they ask. It shows clear understanding.

q.q: What is `box-sizing: border-box`?
a: By default (`content-box`), `width` only sets the content width, and padding and border are added on top. With `border-box`, the width includes padding and border, so a 200px box stays 200px. Most projects set it globally:

q.q: What is the difference between margin and padding?
a: Padding is space inside the border (it gets the element's background colour). Margin is space outside the border (always transparent). Margins can be negative; padding cannot.

q.q: What is margin collapsing?
a: When two vertical margins meet (like a bottom margin of one paragraph and the top margin of the next), they combine into one margin equal to the bigger one instead of adding up. It only happens vertically, not horizontally, and not in flex or grid containers.

q.q: What is the difference between `display: none`, `visibility: hidden` and `opacity: 0`?
a: `display: none` removes the element completely; it takes no space.
`visibility: hidden` hides it but it still takes space.
`opacity: 0` makes it transparent; it takes space and can still be clicked.

q.q: What is the difference between `inline`, `block` and `inline-block`?
a: `block`: new line, full width, width/height work.
`inline`: stays in the line, width/height do not work, vertical margins are ignored.
`inline-block`: stays in the line like inline, but width, height and all margins work.

q.q: Explain the `position` property values.
a: `static`: default, normal flow; top/left do not work.
`relative`: moves relative to its normal position; the original space is kept.
`absolute`: removed from the flow and positioned relative to the nearest positioned (non-static) ancestor.
`fixed`: positioned relative to the browser window; stays when scrolling (sticky navbars, chat buttons).
`sticky`: acts like relative until you scroll to a point, then sticks like fixed.

q.q: What is `z-index`?
a: `z-index` controls which element appears on top when elements overlap. Higher numbers are in front. It only works on positioned elements (not static) or flex/grid items.

q.q: What is the difference between `absolute` and `fixed` positioning?
a: Absolute is positioned relative to the nearest positioned parent and scrolls with the page. Fixed is positioned relative to the viewport and stays in the same place when you scroll.

q.q: What are floats and how do you clear them?
a: `float: left/right` pushes an element to one side so text wraps around it. Parents may collapse because floats leave the normal flow. Fix with `clear: both` on a following element or `display: flow-root` on the parent. Today we use Flexbox/Grid for layout instead.

q.q: What is the `overflow` property?
a: It controls what happens when content is bigger than its box: `visible` (default, spills out), `hidden` (cut off), `scroll` (always shows scrollbars), `auto` (scrollbars only when needed).

q.q: What is Flexbox?
a: Flexbox is a one-dimensional layout system for arranging items in a row or a column. You set `display: flex` on the parent, and its children become flex items that can grow, shrink and align easily.

q.q: What are the main Flexbox properties?
a: `justify-content`: aligns items on the main axis (flex-start, center, space-between, space-around, space-evenly)
`align-items`: aligns items on the cross axis (stretch, center, flex-start, flex-end)
`flex-wrap`: wrap items to the next line

q.q: What is the difference between `justify-content` and `align-items`?
a: `justify-content` aligns items along the main axis (horizontal for a row). `align-items` aligns them along the cross axis (vertical for a row). If you change `flex-direction` to column, the axes swap.

q.q: What does `flex: 1` mean?
a: It is shorthand for `flex-grow: 1; flex-shrink: 1; flex-basis: 0`. All items with `flex: 1` share the available space equally.

q.q: How do you center a div horizontally and vertically?
a: For horizontal-only centering of a block with a width: `margin: 0 auto;`.

q.q: What is CSS Grid?
a: Grid is a two-dimensional layout system that handles rows and columns at the same time. It is great for full page layouts and card galleries.

q.q: What is the difference between Flexbox and Grid?
a: Flexbox is one-dimensional (a row OR a column) and is content-first, ideal for navbars, buttons and aligning items. Grid is two-dimensional (rows AND columns) and is layout-first, ideal for page layouts and galleries. They are often used together.

q.q: What is the `fr` unit?
a: `fr` means "fraction of the free space" in a grid. `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr` makes the second column twice as wide as the first.

q.q: How do you make a responsive grid without media queries?
a: The browser fits as many 200px-minimum columns as possible and stretches them to fill the row.

q.q: What is responsive design?
a: Designing pages that adapt to every screen size: mobile, tablet and desktop. Tools: the viewport meta tag, fluid widths (%), flexible units (rem, vw), Flexbox/Grid, responsive images and media queries.

q.q: What are media queries?
a: Media queries apply CSS only when a condition is true, usually screen width.

q.q: What is the mobile-first approach?
a: You write base styles for small screens first, then add `min-width` media queries for bigger screens. Mobile CSS stays simple and fast, and it matches how most users browse today.

q.q: What is the difference between `px`, `em`, `rem`, `%`, `vh` and `vw`?
a: `em`: relative to the parent's font size (can compound when nested).
`rem`: relative to the root (`html`) font size; predictable, best for fonts and spacing.

q.q: What is the difference between `min-width`, `max-width` and `width`?
a: `width` sets a fixed size. `max-width` says "never bigger than this" and lets the element shrink on small screens, which is great for responsiveness (`max-width: 100%` on images). `min-width` says "never smaller than this".

q.q: What is the difference between transition and animation?
a: A **transition** smoothly changes a property from one value to another when the state changes (like on hover); it needs a trigger. An **animation** uses `@keyframes`, can have many steps, can loop and can start on its own.

q.q: What is the `transform` property?
a: It changes an element's shape or position without affecting the layout around it: `translate()`, `rotate()`, `scale()`, `skew()`. Transforms and opacity are the cheapest properties to animate because they don't trigger layout.

q.q: What are CSS variables (custom properties)?
a: Reusable values defined with `--name` and used with `var()`.
They can be changed at runtime with JS and are commonly used for themes like dark mode.

q.q: What are `::before` and `::after` used for?
a: They insert decorative content before or after an element's content using the `content` property, e.g. icons, quotes, overlays or custom bullets, without adding extra HTML.

q.q: How do you add a gradient background?
a:
background: linear-gradient(to right, #ff7e5f, #feb47b);
background: radial-gradient(circle, white, skyblue);

q.q: What is the difference between `rgba` and `opacity`?
a: `rgba(0,0,0,0.5)` makes only that colour semi-transparent (like the background), while `opacity: 0.5` makes the entire element, including its text and children, semi-transparent.

q.q: What are CSS preprocessors?
a: Tools like **Sass/SCSS** and **Less** that add variables, nesting, mixins and functions to CSS. They compile into normal CSS. Native CSS now supports variables and nesting too.

q.q: What is Tailwind CSS and how is it different from Bootstrap?
a: Tailwind is a utility-first framework: you style by combining small classes like `flex p-4 text-center bg-blue-500`. Bootstrap gives ready-made components like `.btn` and `.navbar`. Tailwind gives more design freedom; Bootstrap is faster for standard-looking UIs.

q.q: What is BEM?
a: BEM (Block, Element, Modifier) is a class naming convention that keeps CSS organised: `.card`, `.card__title`, `.card--featured`. It avoids naming clashes in large projects.

q.q: What is the difference between `reset.css` and `normalize.css`?
a: Reset removes all browser default styles (margins, heading sizes) so you start from zero. Normalize keeps useful defaults and only fixes inconsistencies between browsers.

q.q: What are reflow and repaint?
a: **Reflow** (layout) happens when the size or position of elements changes and the browser recalculates the layout. It is expensive. **Repaint** happens when only looks change (like colour) and is cheaper. Animate `transform` and `opacity` to avoid reflow.

q.q: How do you improve CSS performance?
a: Minify CSS, remove unused CSS, avoid very deep selectors, load critical CSS first, avoid `@import` chains, and animate only `transform`/`opacity`.

q.q: What is `object-fit`?
a: It controls how an `` or `

q.q: What are `nth-child` and `nth-of-type`?
a: `li:nth-child(2)` selects the second child if it is an `li`. `p:nth-of-type(2)` selects the second `p` among its siblings, ignoring other tags. `nth-child(odd)` or `(2n)` is used for striped tables.

q.q: How do you make text truncate with "..."?
a: .title { white-space: nowrap; overflow: hidden; text-overflow: ellipsis; }

q.q: What is the `:root` selector?
a: `:root` targets the top-level `<html>` element but with higher specificity. It is the usual place to define global CSS variables.

q.q: How would you build a dark mode?
a: Define colours as CSS variables in `:root`, then override them for a dark theme, either with a `.dark` class on `<html>` or the `prefers-color-scheme: dark` media query. Toggle the class with JavaScript and save the choice in localStorage.

q.q: What is the difference between `visibility: hidden` and `display: none` for accessibility?
a: Both hide the element from screen readers. If you want text hidden visually but still read by screen readers (like a "skip to content" label), use a visually-hidden class (position absolute, 1px size, clip) instead.

q.q: What is the difference between `position: relative` on a parent and `absolute` on a child?
a: This is the most common positioning pattern. The parent gets `position: relative` (without moving it) so it becomes the reference box. The child with `position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;` is then placed at the parent's top-right corner, e.g. a badge on a card or a close button on a modal.

q.q: What is `calc()`?
a: A CSS function that does math with mixed units: `width: calc(100% - 250px);` makes a main area that fills the space next to a 250px sidebar.

q.q: What are `clamp()`, `min()` and `max()`?
a: `clamp(min, preferred, max)` keeps a value within a range, great for fluid font sizes: `font-size: clamp(1rem, 2.5vw, 2rem);`. `min()` picks the smaller value and `max()` the larger.

q.q: What is the `:has()` selector?
a: A "parent selector" that styles an element based on what it contains: `.card:has(img)` styles only cards that contain an image. It's supported in all modern browsers.

sub: Covers JSX, components, props and state, hooks (useState, useEffect, useContext, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, custom hooks), the virtual DOM, routing, Redux and performance. Matches what was reported in MERN fresher drives (Tech Mahindra, startups) and frontend rounds.

q.q: What is React?
a: React is an open-source JavaScript library made by Meta for building user interfaces, especially single-page applications. You build the UI from small reusable pieces called **components**, and React updates the page efficiently when data changes.

q.q: What are the main features of React?
a: One-way data flow (parent to child via props)
Hooks for state and side effects

q.q: What is JSX?
a: JSX is a syntax that lets you write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. Babel converts it into `React.createElement()` calls.
Rules: return one parent element (or a Fragment), use `className` instead of `class`, close all tags, and put JS expressions inside `{ }`.

q.q: What is the Virtual DOM and how does it work?
a: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight copy of the real DOM kept in memory. When state changes:
1. React creates a new virtual DOM tree.
2. It compares it with the previous one (this is called **diffing**).
3. It updates only the changed parts in the real DOM (this is **reconciliation**).
Updating the real DOM is slow, so touching only what changed makes React fast.

q.q: What is the difference between the real DOM and the virtual DOM?
a: The real DOM is what the browser shows; updating it is slow and causes re-layout. The virtual DOM is a JS object in memory; it is cheap to create and compare, and React uses it to work out the smallest set of real DOM updates.

q.q: What is a Single Page Application (SPA)?
a: An SPA loads one HTML page once and then updates the content with JavaScript, without full page reloads. Gmail and most React apps are SPAs. Pros: fast, app-like feel. Cons: slower first load and weaker SEO unless you use SSR (e.g. Next.js).

q.q: What are components? What are the types?
a: Components are reusable, independent pieces of UI, like a Navbar or a Card.
**Functional components**: plain JS functions that return JSX; use hooks for state. This is the modern standard.
**Class components**: ES6 classes that extend `React.Component`, use `this.state` and lifecycle methods. Older style.

q.q: What is the difference between props and state?
a: **Props** are inputs passed from parent to child. They are read-only for the child.
**State** is data owned and managed inside the component. When state changes, the component re-renders.

q.q: What is the difference between class and functional components?
a: Class components use `this.state`, `setState`, and lifecycle methods like `componentDidMount`. Functional components are simpler functions and use hooks (`useState`, `useEffect`) for the same features. Functional components have less code, no `this` confusion, and are recommended today.

q.q: What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
a: Prop drilling is passing props through many layers of components that don't need them, just to reach a deep child. Avoid it with the **Context API**, a state library like **Redux** or **Zustand**, or by restructuring components (component composition).

q.q: What are keys in React and why are they important?
a: Keys are unique identifiers for list items. They help React know which items changed, were added or were removed, so it updates efficiently.
Avoid using the array index as key if the list can change order, because it can cause bugs.

q.q: What is a React Fragment?
a: A Fragment lets you return multiple elements without adding an extra `<div>` to the DOM. Written as `<React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>` or `<>...</>`.

q.q: What is conditional rendering?
a: Showing different UI based on a condition.

q.q: What are controlled and uncontrolled components?
a: In a **controlled** component, the form value lives in React state and changes through `onChange`. In an **uncontrolled** component, the DOM keeps the value and you read it with a `ref`.

const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />
Controlled is preferred because React stays the single source of truth.

q.q: What is lifting state up?
a: When two sibling components need the same data, you move that state to their common parent and pass it down as props. This keeps them in sync.

q.q: What is one-way data binding in React?
a: Data flows only from parent to child through props. A child cannot directly change the parent's data; it calls a function passed by the parent instead. This makes data flow predictable and easier to debug.

q.q: What are synthetic events?
a: React wraps browser events in its own `SyntheticEvent` object so events behave the same in every browser. You use them like normal: `onClick`, `onChange`, `e.preventDefault()`.

q.q: What are hooks? What are the rules of hooks?
a: Hooks are functions that let functional components use state and other React features. Common ones: `useState`, `useEffect`, `useContext`, `useRef`, `useMemo`, `useCallback`, `useReducer`.
Call hooks only at the top level, never inside loops, conditions or nested functions.
Call hooks only from React function components or custom hooks.

q.q: Explain `useState`.
a: `useState` adds state to a functional component. It returns the current value and a function to update it.
Updating state triggers a re-render. State updates are asynchronous and batched.

q.q: Explain `useEffect` and its dependency array.
a: `useEffect` runs side effects like API calls, timers and subscriptions after the component renders.
No array: runs after every render.
`[]` empty array: runs once after the first render (like componentDidMount).
The function you return is the **cleanup**, which runs before the next effect or on unmount (like componentWillUnmount).

q.q: What is the Context API and `useContext`?
a: Context shares data (like theme, logged-in user, language) with many components without passing props manually at every level.
A Tech Mahindra candidate was asked to write useContext pseudo-code. Practise writing the 3 steps: create, provide, consume.

q.q: What is `useRef`?
a: `useRef` returns an object `{ current: value }` that stays the same between renders. Changing it does NOT cause a re-render. Uses: accessing DOM elements (focus an input) and storing values like timer IDs or the previous value.

q.q: What is the difference between `useMemo` and `useCallback`?
a: Both are for performance and both take a dependency array.
`useMemo` caches a **computed value**: `const total = useMemo(() => calcTotal(items), [items]);`
`useCallback` caches a **function** so it is not recreated on every render: `const handle = useCallback(() => {...}, [id]);`
Use them only when there is a real performance problem.

q.q: What is `useReducer`?
a: An alternative to `useState` for complex state with many actions. You write a reducer function `(state, action) => newState` and call `dispatch({ type: "add" })`. It is similar to how Redux works.

q.q: What is a custom hook?
a: A custom hook is your own function starting with `use` that reuses stateful logic across components.

q.q: What is the difference between `useEffect` and `useLayoutEffect`?
a: `useEffect` runs after the browser paints the screen (non-blocking). `useLayoutEffect` runs after DOM changes but before painting; use it only when you must measure or change the layout without a visible flicker.

q.q: Why should you not update state directly?
a: Writing `this.state.count = 5` or mutating an array in state does not tell React anything changed, so the UI won't re-render. Always use the setter and create new objects/arrays: `setItems([...items, newItem])`.

q.q: What are the lifecycle methods of a class component?
a: In functional components, `useEffect` covers all three.

q.q: When does a React component re-render?
a: When its state changes, when its props change, when its parent re-renders, or when a context it uses changes.

q.q: What is `React.memo`?
a: `React.memo` wraps a functional component so it re-renders only when its props actually change. It is like `PureComponent` for class components.

const Card = React.memo(function Card({ title }) { return

{title}

; });

q.q: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC)?
a: An HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra features, e.g. `withAuth(Dashboard)` that checks login first. Hooks have replaced most HOC use cases.

q.q: What is reconciliation and the diffing algorithm?
a: Reconciliation is how React decides what to change in the DOM. The diffing algorithm assumes: elements of different types produce different trees (so it replaces them), and keys identify list items. This makes comparing trees fast (O(n)).

q.q: What is React Fiber?
a: Fiber is React's internal engine (since React 16). It splits rendering work into small units, so React can pause, prioritise and resume work, which keeps the app responsive during big updates.

q.q: What is StrictMode?
a: `<React.StrictMode>` is a development-only tool that highlights potential problems. It renders components twice in development to catch side-effect bugs. It does nothing in production.

q.q: What is React Router? How do you set up routes?
a: React Router handles navigation between pages in an SPA without reloading.

<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/user/:id" element={<User />} />
    <Route path="*" element={<NotFound />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>
Use `<Link to="/about">` instead of `<a>`, `useParams()` to read `:id`, and `useNavigate()` to redirect in code.

q.q: How do you call an API in React?
a: Use `fetch` or `axios` inside `useEffect`, store the result in state, and handle loading and errors.

q.q: How do you handle forms in React?
a: Use controlled inputs with state, an `onSubmit` handler with `e.preventDefault()`, and validation. For big forms, libraries like **React Hook Form** or **Formik** help.

q.q: How do you implement protected routes?
a: Create a wrapper component that checks if the user is logged in (from context or Redux). If yes, render the page; if not, redirect with `<Navigate to="/login" />`.

q.q: What is Redux and why use it?
a: Redux is a library to manage global state in one central **store**. It is useful when many components share data. Core ideas:
**Action**: an object describing what happened, `{ type: "cart/add", payload: item }`.
**Reducer**: a pure function that returns new state based on the action.
**Dispatch**: sends an action to the store.
Today, **Redux Toolkit** is the recommended way; it reduces boilerplate with `createSlice` and `configureStore`.

q.q: What is the difference between Context API and Redux?
a: Context is built-in and good for small amounts of rarely-changing global data (theme, user). Redux is better for large apps with complex, frequently-updated state, and gives devtools, middleware and predictable patterns.

q.q: What are `useSelector` and `useDispatch`?
a: Hooks from react-redux. `useSelector(state => state.cart.items)` reads data from the store. `useDispatch()` returns the dispatch function to send actions.

q.q: How do you optimise a React app's performance?
a: Use `React.memo`, `useMemo` and `useCallback` to avoid unnecessary re-renders.
Keep state as local as possible.
Optimise images and use the production build.

q.q: What is lazy loading / code splitting in React?
a: Loading a component only when it's needed, instead of in the first bundle.

q.q: What are error boundaries?
a: Components that catch JavaScript errors in their child tree and show a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. They must be class components using `componentDidCatch` or `getDerivedStateFromError` (or use the react-error-boundary library).

q.q: What are portals?
a: `createPortal(child, domNode)` renders a child into a different DOM node outside the parent, which is useful for modals, tooltips and popups that must appear above everything.

q.q: What is the difference between React and Angular?
a: React is a library focused on the UI layer, uses JSX and one-way data flow, and you pick other tools yourself. Angular is a full framework by Google with TypeScript, two-way binding, dependency injection and built-in routing.

q.q: What is Create React App vs Vite?
a: Both create a React project setup. CRA (now deprecated) used Webpack. **Vite** is the modern choice: it uses native ES modules in development, so it starts and reloads much faster.

q.q: What is the difference between server-side rendering (SSR) and client-side rendering (CSR)?
a: In CSR, the browser gets an almost empty HTML and JS builds the page, so the first view is slower and SEO is weaker. In SSR, the server sends fully built HTML, so the first view is faster and SEO is better. Next.js adds SSR to React.

q.q: What are React Server Components?
a: Components that run only on the server (React 19, Next.js App Router). They can fetch data directly and send ready HTML with zero JS to the browser, which makes pages lighter. Interactive parts are marked as Client Components with `"use client"`.

q.q: What is the difference between state and props in terms of who can change them?
a: Props are owned by the parent and are read-only in the child. State is owned by the component itself and changed with its setter. If a child must change parent data, the parent passes down a callback function as a prop.

q.q: Why does `setState` / `setCount` not update the value immediately?
a: State updates are scheduled and batched for performance, so reading the variable right after calling the setter still shows the old value. Use the updater form `setCount(c => c + 1)` when the new value depends on the old one, or `useEffect` to react after the update.

q.q: What is the `children` prop?
a: Whatever you put between a component's opening and closing tags is passed as `props.children`. It's used to build wrapper components like `<Card>`, `<Modal>` or layouts.

sub: Covers the Node runtime, event loop, modules, npm, streams and buffers, file system, async patterns, error handling, clustering, security and authentication basics, as asked in backend and MERN rounds.

q.q: What is Node.js?
a: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime built on Chrome's **V8 engine** that lets you run JavaScript outside the browser, mainly on servers. It is single-threaded, event-driven and uses non-blocking I/O, which makes it great for APIs, real-time apps (chat) and handling many connections at once.

q.q: Is Node.js single-threaded? How does it handle many requests?
a: Your JavaScript code runs on a single main thread. But slow work like file reading, database calls and network requests is handed off to the system or to **libuv's thread pool**. While that work happens, Node keeps accepting new requests. When the work finishes, its callback is put in a queue and the **event loop** runs it. So one thread can serve thousands of users, as long as you don't block it with heavy CPU work.

q.q: What is the event loop in Node.js?
a: The event loop is the mechanism that lets Node do non-blocking I/O on a single thread. It continuously checks for completed tasks and runs their callbacks in phases:
**Poll**: gets new I/O events and runs their callbacks.
Between each phase, Node runs microtasks: `process.nextTick` first, then resolved promises.

q.q: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking code?
a: Blocking code stops everything until it finishes, e.g. `fs.readFileSync`. Non-blocking code starts the task and moves on, and a callback/promise handles the result later, e.g. `fs.readFile` or `fs.promises.readFile`. In a server you should use non-blocking code so one slow request doesn't freeze all users.

q.q: What is libuv?
a: libuv is a C library used by Node that provides the event loop, the thread pool (default 4 threads) and asynchronous handling of files, DNS, networking and timers across operating systems.

q.q: What is V8?
a: V8 is Google's open-source JavaScript engine (used in Chrome). It compiles JavaScript into machine code using JIT (just-in-time) compilation, which makes Node fast.

q.q: Where is Node.js a bad choice?
a: For CPU-heavy work like video encoding, big image processing or heavy calculations, because they block the single thread. You can use worker threads, or another language for such services.

q.q: What is the difference between Node.js and a browser's JavaScript?
a: Both use JavaScript, but the browser has the DOM, `window` and `document`, while Node has no DOM and instead provides modules for files (`fs`), servers (`http`), OS info and processes. The global object is `window` in the browser and `global`/`globalThis` in Node.

q.q: What are modules in Node.js? What are the types?
a: A module is a reusable file of code. Types:

q.q: What is the difference between `require` and `import`?
a: `require` is the CommonJS syntax (`module.exports`), loads modules synchronously and can be called anywhere. `import`/`export` is the ES Module syntax, is static (top of the file), supports tree-shaking and is the modern standard. To use ESM in Node, set `"type": "module"` in package.json or use `.mjs` files.

q.q: What is the difference between `module.exports` and `exports`?
a: `exports` is just a shortcut reference to `module.exports`. You can add properties to it (`exports.add = ...`), but if you assign a new value to `exports` directly, the link breaks. What actually gets exported is always `module.exports`.

q.q: What is npm and what is package.json?
a: npm (Node Package Manager) installs and manages third-party packages. `package.json` describes your project: name, version, scripts (`npm start`, `npm run dev`), dependencies and devDependencies.

q.q: What is the difference between dependencies and devDependencies?
a: `dependencies` are needed to run the app in production (express, mongoose). `devDependencies` are only needed during development (nodemon, jest, eslint). Install a dev one with `npm install -D nodemon`.

q.q: What is package-lock.json?
a: It records the exact versions of every installed package and sub-package, so every developer and server installs exactly the same versions. You should commit it to Git.

q.q: What is the difference between npm and npx?
a: `npm` installs packages. `npx` runs a package's command without installing it globally, e.g. `npx create-vite@latest`.

q.q: What does `^` and `~` mean in package versions?
a: `^1.4.2` allows updates to any 1.x.x version (minor and patch). `~1.4.2` allows only patch updates (1.4.x). No symbol means an exact version.

q.q: How do you create a simple HTTP server in Node.js?
How do you read and write files in Node.js?
a: There are also sync versions (`readFileSync`) and callback versions (`fs.readFile(path, cb)`).

q.q: What is the `path` module used for?
a: To work with file paths safely across operating systems: `path.join(__dirname, "public", "index.html")`, `path.extname("a.png")`, `path.basename()`.

q.q: What are `__dirname` and `__filename`?
a: `__dirname` is the absolute path of the folder containing the current file, and `__filename` is the absolute path of the file itself. They exist in CommonJS; in ES modules use `import.meta.dirname` (newer Node) or `fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)`.

q.q: What is the EventEmitter?
a: The `events` module lets objects emit named events and other code listen to them. Many Node features (streams, HTTP server) are built on it.

q.q: What is the `process` object?
a: A global object with information about the running Node process: `process.env` (environment variables), `process.argv` (command-line arguments), `process.exit()`, `process.pid`, and `process.on("uncaughtException")`.

q.q: What is the `os` module?
a: It gives information about the operating system: `os.cpus()`, `os.totalmem()`, `os.freemem()`, `os.platform()`, `os.hostname()`.

q.q: What are streams? What are the types?
a: Streams process data piece by piece (in chunks) instead of loading it all into memory, which is ideal for big files and videos. Types:
**Writable**: you write to it (`fs.createWriteStream`, HTTP response).
**Transform**: duplex that changes data on the way (zlib compression).

q.q: What is a Buffer?
a: A Buffer is a fixed-size chunk of raw binary data in memory. Node uses buffers to handle data from files, networks and streams before it's converted to strings. `Buffer.from("hello")`.

q.q: What is piping?
a: `readable.pipe(writable)` connects a readable stream to a writable stream so data flows automatically. It also handles backpressure (slowing down when the writer is busy). `stream.pipeline()` is a safer version with error handling.

q.q: What is the difference between `process.nextTick()`, `setImmediate()` and `setTimeout()`?
a: `process.nextTick()` runs right after the current operation, before any other I/O or timers (highest priority).
`setImmediate()` runs in the check phase, after I/O.
Inside an I/O callback, `setImmediate` always runs before `setTimeout(fn, 0)`.

q.q: What is callback hell and how do you fix it?
a: Deeply nested callbacks, each depending on the previous one, that become hard to read and handle errors in. Fix it with promises, `async/await`, `util.promisify`, and by breaking code into small functions.

q.q: How do you handle errors in Node.js?
a: Callbacks: check the first `err` argument (error-first callbacks).
Global safety nets: `process.on("unhandledRejection")` and `process.on("uncaughtException")` to log and restart the process.

q.q: What is an error-first callback?
a: A Node convention where the first argument of a callback is the error and the second is the result.

q.q: What is `util.promisify`?
a: It converts a callback-based function into one that returns a promise, so you can use `await` with it: `const readFile = util.promisify(fs.readFile);`.

q.q: What is clustering in Node.js?
a: Node runs on one CPU core by default. The `cluster` module (or PM2 in cluster mode) starts multiple worker processes, one per core, that share the same port. This uses all CPU cores and improves throughput. If one worker crashes, others continue.

q.q: What are worker threads?
a: `worker_threads` let you run CPU-heavy JavaScript in parallel threads within the same process, so the main event loop is not blocked. Use them for heavy calculations, not for I/O.

q.q: What is the difference between cluster and worker threads?
a: Cluster creates separate processes, each with its own memory and event loop, mostly to handle more requests. Worker threads are threads inside one process that can share memory, mostly for CPU-heavy tasks.

q.q: What is PM2?
a: PM2 is a production process manager for Node. It keeps your app running, restarts it after crashes, runs it in cluster mode, manages logs and can start the app on server reboot.

q.q: How do you improve Node.js performance?
a: Avoid blocking code, use async I/O, cache with Redis, use clustering/PM2, compress responses (gzip), use streams for large data, add database indexes, and use pagination.

q.q: What is a memory leak in Node and how do you find it?
a: A memory leak happens when memory is used but never freed, often from global variables, ever-growing caches/arrays, or event listeners that are never removed. Find it by watching memory usage over time and taking heap snapshots with Chrome DevTools (`node --inspect`).

q.q: What are environment variables and how do you use them?
a: Values set outside the code, like DB URLs, API keys and the port, so secrets aren't committed to Git. Store them in a `.env` file (added to `.gitignore`) and load them with `dotenv` (or `node --env-file=.env` in newer Node). Read them with `process.env.MONGO_URI`.

q.q: What is JWT and how does JWT authentication work?
a: JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token with three parts: header, payload, signature.
1. The user logs in with email/password.
2. The server checks the password and creates a token: `jwt.sign({ id: user._id }, SECRET, { expiresIn: "1d" })`.
3. The client stores the token (preferably in an httpOnly cookie) and sends it with each request.
4. The server verifies it with `jwt.verify()` in middleware before giving access.
It is stateless, so the server does not need to store sessions.

q.q: How do you store passwords securely?
a: Never store plain passwords. Hash them with **bcrypt** (which adds a salt automatically), then compare during login.

const hash = await bcrypt.hash(password, 10);
const ok = await bcrypt.compare(inputPassword, hash);

q.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
a: Authentication checks **who you are** (login). Authorization checks **what you are allowed to do** (e.g. only admins can delete users).

q.q: What is CORS?
a: CORS (Cross-Origin Resource Sharing) is a browser security rule that blocks a page from calling an API on a different origin (domain/port) unless the server allows it. In Express, use the `cors` package: `app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173" }))`.

q.q: What are common security practices in Node apps?
a: Validate and sanitise input, hash passwords, use HTTPS, set secure headers with **helmet**, add rate limiting, keep secrets in env variables, avoid `eval`, update packages (`npm audit`), and use parameterised queries to prevent injection.

q.q: What is REST? What are the HTTP methods?
a: REST is a style for designing APIs around resources using standard HTTP methods:
`GET /users` read, `POST /users` create, `PUT /users/1` replace, `PATCH /users/1` partial update, `DELETE /users/1` remove.
REST APIs are stateless and usually return JSON.

q.q: What are common HTTP status codes?
a: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content, 301 Moved, 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (no permission), 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict, 429 Too Many Requests, 500 Internal Server Error.

q.q: What are WebSockets and Socket.io?
a: WebSockets keep a two-way, always-open connection between client and server, so the server can push data instantly. Socket.io is a popular Node library built on WebSockets for chat apps, live notifications and multiplayer games.

q.q: What is nodemon?
a: A development tool that restarts your Node server automatically whenever you save a file. Newer Node versions also have `node --watch`.

q.q: What is middleware?
a: A function that runs between receiving a request and sending the response, used for logging, authentication, parsing JSON and error handling. It is a core concept in Express (see the Express document).

q.q: What is the difference between `fs.readFile` and `fs.createReadStream`?
a: `readFile` loads the whole file into memory before you can use it, which is fine for small files. `createReadStream` reads it in small chunks, so memory stays low even for multi-GB files, and you can start sending data immediately.

q.q: How do you handle graceful shutdown in Node?
a: Listen for `SIGTERM`/`SIGINT`, stop accepting new requests with `server.close()`, finish in-flight requests, close the database connection, then `process.exit(0)`. This prevents lost requests during deploys.

q.q: What is the difference between `spawn`, `exec` and `fork`?
a: All are in `child_process`. `exec` runs a command and buffers the whole output (good for small outputs). `spawn` streams the output (good for large outputs or long processes). `fork` starts a new Node process with a message channel to talk to the parent.

q.q: What is caching and how do you use Redis with Node?
a: Caching stores frequently requested data in fast memory so the database isn't hit every time. With Redis, check the cache first; if the key is missing, query the DB, save the result in Redis with an expiry (`SET key value EX 60`), and return it.

sub: Covers routing, middleware, request/response, REST API design, error handling, authentication with JWT, file uploads, validation, security and project structure for MERN backend interviews.

q.q: What is Express.js?
a: Express is a minimal and flexible web framework for Node.js. It makes building servers and REST APIs much easier than plain `http` by giving simple routing, middleware support, and helpers for requests and responses. It is the "E" in MERN.

q.q: Why use Express instead of the plain Node http module?
a: With plain `http`, you must manually parse URLs, read request bodies, set headers and handle routes using if-else. Express gives clean routing (`app.get`), middleware, JSON parsing, static files, and error handling with very little code.

q.q: How do you create a basic Express server?
What is the difference between `app.listen` and `http.createServer(app)`?
a: `app.listen()` creates the HTTP server for you. You use `http.createServer(app)` when you need direct access to the server object, e.g. to attach Socket.io.

q.q: What is routing in Express?
a: Routing decides how the app responds to a request based on the URL path and HTTP method.

q.q: What is the difference between `req.params`, `req.query` and `req.body`?
a: `req.params`: values from the URL path. `/users/:id` with `/users/42` gives `req.params.id = "42"`.
`req.body`: data sent in the request body (POST/PUT). It needs `express.json()` middleware.

q.q: What is `express.Router()`?
a: Router creates modular, mountable route handlers so you can split routes into separate files.

q.q: What are route parameters and how do you make one optional?
a: Route parameters are named URL segments like `:id`. In Express 4 you can make one optional with `?`: `/users/:id?`. Express 5 changed the path syntax and uses braces for optional parts: `/users{/:id}`.

q.q: How do you handle 404 routes?
a: Add a middleware after all routes; it runs only if no route matched.
app.use((req, res) => res.status(404).json({ message: "Route not found" }));

q.q: What is `app.all()` and `app.route()`?
a: `app.all("/x", fn)` handles every HTTP method on a path. `app.route("/users").get(fn).post(fn)` chains handlers for one path, avoiding repeated paths.

q.q: What is middleware in Express?
a: Middleware is a function that has access to `req`, `res` and `next`. It runs in the middle of the request-response cycle and can change the request, end the response, or call `next()` to pass control to the next middleware.

q.q: What are the types of middleware?
a: **Error-handling**: has four arguments `(err, req, res, next)`.

q.q: What does `next()` do? What happens if you don't call it?
a: `next()` passes control to the next middleware or route handler. If you neither call `next()` nor send a response, the request hangs until it times out. `next(err)` skips to the error-handling middleware.

q.q: Does the order of middleware matter?
a: Yes. Express runs middleware in the order you add them. For example, `express.json()` must come before routes that read `req.body`, and the 404 and error handlers must come last.

q.q: What is `express.static()`?
a: It serves static files like HTML, CSS, images and the React build folder directly. `app.use(express.static("public"))` makes `public/logo.png` available at `/logo.png`.

q.q: What is the difference between `express.json()` and `express.urlencoded()`?
a: `express.json()` parses requests with a JSON body (`Content-Type: application/json`), used by React/fetch. `express.urlencoded({ extended: true })` parses HTML form submissions (`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`).

q.q: What is morgan?
a: A logging middleware that prints each request's method, URL, status and response time in the console: `app.use(morgan("dev"))`.

q.q: What is the difference between `res.send()`, `res.json()` and `res.end()`?
a: `res.send()` sends any type (string, HTML, object) and sets the content type automatically.
`res.json()` sends JSON and sets `Content-Type: application/json`. Best for APIs.
`res.end()` ends the response without data (comes from Node).

q.q: How do you set status codes?
What is the "Cannot set headers after they are sent" error?
a: It happens when you try to send a response twice for one request, usually because you forgot to `return` after an early `res.json()`.

if (!user) return res.status(404).json({ msg: "No user" });
res.json(user);

q.q: How do you redirect in Express?
How do you read headers and cookies?
a: Headers: `req.headers.authorization` or `req.get("Authorization")`. Cookies: use `cookie-parser` then `req.cookies.token`. Set cookies with `res.cookie("token", t, { httpOnly: true })`.

q.q: How do you handle errors in Express?
a: Create an error-handling middleware with 4 parameters, placed after all routes:

q.q: How do you handle errors in async route handlers?
a: In Express 4, errors thrown in async functions are not caught automatically, so you wrap them with try/catch or a helper.
Express 5 forwards rejected promises to the error handler automatically.

q.q: What is a custom error class?
a: A class extending `Error` with a status code, so you can throw meaningful errors: `throw new AppError("User not found", 404)`, and the error middleware reads `err.statusCode`.

q.q: How would you design a REST API for a to-do app?
a:
GET    /api/todos        -> list all
GET    /api/todos/:id    -> get one
POST   /api/todos        -> create
PATCH  /api/todos/:id    -> update (e.g. mark done)
DELETE /api/todos/:id    -> delete
Use nouns (not verbs) in URLs, correct HTTP methods and status codes, JSON responses, and consistent error formats.

q.q: What is the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a: PUT replaces the whole resource with what you send. PATCH updates only the fields you send. Example: to change only the title of a todo, use PATCH.

q.q: What does stateless mean in REST?
a: Each request contains everything the server needs (like the auth token). The server does not remember previous requests, which makes it easier to scale across many servers.

q.q: What is the MVC pattern in Express?
a: **View**: what the user sees (React frontend, or a template engine).
**Controller**: logic that handles a request, talks to the model and sends the response.

q.q: How do you implement pagination?
a: Read `page` and `limit` from the query string and use skip/limit in the database.

q.q: How do you implement search and filtering?
a: Read filters from `req.query` and build the database query: `Product.find({ category: req.query.category, price: { $lte: req.query.max } })`. For text search, use a regex or a text index.

q.q: What is API versioning?
a: Putting a version in the URL (`/api/v1/users`) or a header, so you can change the API later without breaking old clients.

q.q: How do you implement JWT authentication in Express?
a: 1. **Register**: hash the password with bcrypt and save the user.
2. **Login**: find the user, compare the password, and send a JWT.

q.q: How do you implement role-based access (admin routes)?
a: After the auth middleware, add a middleware that checks the role.

const adminOnly = (req, res, next) =>
  req.user.role === "admin" ? next() : res.status(403).json({ msg: "Forbidden" });

q.q: What is the difference between sessions and JWT?
a: Sessions store login data on the server and give the browser a session ID cookie. JWT stores the data inside a signed token on the client, so the server stays stateless. Sessions are easier to revoke; JWTs scale more easily.

q.q: How do you enable CORS in Express?
a:
const cors = require("cors");
app.use(cors({ origin: "http://localhost:5173", credentials: true }));
This adds headers like `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` so the browser allows the frontend to call the API.

q.q: What is helmet?
a: A middleware that sets secure HTTP headers (like Content-Security-Policy and X-Frame-Options) to protect against common attacks such as clickjacking and XSS.

q.q: How do you add rate limiting?
a: Use `express-rate-limit` to restrict how many requests one IP can make in a time window, which protects login routes from brute-force attacks.

q.q: How do you validate request data?
a: Use libraries like **express-validator**, **Joi** or **Zod** to check fields (required, email format, length) before saving, and return a 400 with clear messages on failure.

q.q: How do you upload files in Express?
a: In production, files are usually uploaded to cloud storage like AWS S3 or Cloudinary.

q.q: How do you connect Express to MongoDB?
What is a template engine?
a: A tool like EJS, Pug or Handlebars that renders HTML on the server with dynamic data: `res.render("profile", { user })`. In MERN apps, React usually replaces this.

q.q: How do you serve a React build from Express?
a: The catch-all route lets React Router handle frontend URLs. In Express 5 the wildcard must be named, e.g. `app.get("/*splat", ...)`.

q.q: How do you test an Express API?
a: Manually with **Postman** or Thunder Client. Automatically with **Jest** + **Supertest**, which can send requests to your app and check the status and body.

q.q: How would you deploy an Express app?
a: Push the code to GitHub, set environment variables on the host, and deploy on Render, Railway, or an AWS EC2 instance (with PM2 and Nginx as a reverse proxy). Use MongoDB Atlas for the database.

q.q: What is the difference between Express and NestJS?
a: Express is minimal and unopinionated; you decide the structure. NestJS is a full framework on top of Express (or Fastify) that uses TypeScript, modules, decorators and dependency injection, making large codebases more organised.

q.q: What is `app.locals` and `res.locals`?
a: `app.locals` stores values available across the whole app (like the site name). `res.locals` stores values only for the current request, often set by middleware for later handlers to use.

q.q: What is the `trust proxy` setting?
a: When your app sits behind a proxy like Nginx or a cloud load balancer, `app.set("trust proxy", 1)` tells Express to read the real client IP and protocol from proxy headers. It matters for rate limiting and secure cookies.

q.q: How would you structure an Express + MongoDB project?
a:
server/
  config/db.js          -> database connection
  models/User.js        -> Mongoose schemas
  controllers/userController.js -> logic
  routes/userRoutes.js  -> URL to controller mapping
  middleware/auth.js    -> JWT check, error handler
  utils/                -> helpers
  server.js             -> app setup, middleware, listen
  .env
Keeping routes thin and logic in controllers (or services) makes the code easy to test and maintain.

q.q: What is the difference between `app.use()` and `app.get()`?
a: `app.use(path, fn)` runs for every HTTP method and matches any path that starts with the given path (used for middleware and mounting routers). `app.get(path, fn)` only handles GET requests on that exact path.

q.q: How do you handle cookies securely?
a: Set `httpOnly: true` (JS can't read it, protects against XSS), `secure: true` (HTTPS only), `sameSite: "strict"` or `"lax"` (protects against CSRF), and an expiry with `maxAge`.

q.q: What is the difference between Express 4 and Express 5?
a: Express 5 automatically forwards errors from async handlers/rejected promises to the error middleware, uses an updated path-matching syntax (wildcards must be named, optional segments use braces), removes some old deprecated methods, and requires a newer Node version.

sub: Covers the App Router, file-based routing, Server and Client Components, rendering strategies (SSR, SSG, ISR, CSR), data fetching and caching, Server Actions, route handlers, SEO, images, auth and deployment. Based on current (App Router) interview question sets.

q.q: What is Next.js?
a: Next.js is a React framework made by Vercel. React only builds the UI; Next.js adds everything else needed for a production app: file-based routing, server-side rendering, static generation, API routes, image and font optimisation, and SEO features.

q.q: What is the difference between React and Next.js?
a: React is a **library** for UI; Next.js is a **framework** built on React.
React apps (Vite/CRA) render on the client by default; Next.js can render on the server (better SEO and faster first load).
React needs React Router; Next.js has built-in file-based routing.
Next.js can also write backend endpoints (route handlers) in the same project.

q.q: What are the advantages of Next.js?
a: Better SEO with SSR/SSG, faster first load, file-based routing, built-in API routes, automatic code splitting, image optimisation with `next/image`, easy deployment on Vercel, and support for TypeScript out of the box.

q.q: How do you create a Next.js project?
a: `npx create-next-app@latest my-app`. It asks about TypeScript, ESLint, Tailwind and the App Router, then creates the project. Run it with `npm run dev`.

q.q: What is the App Router? How is it different from the Pages Router?
